\chapter{Sexto ao Decimo}
\label{ch:pt-ordinais-ate-decimo}
\hlchaptermodality{28}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can count in order all the way to tenth, say why oitavo and nono break the pattern in different ways, and read an ordinal written as a digit with a raised letter.}

The written ordinal -- digit plus a raised letter that agrees in gender -- put against the ten spoken words the two chapters taught.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[sexto / sexta]{sexto — the sixth, and where the numbering stops}

\label{lesson:PT-C28-sexto}



\begin{quote}
Recalls open the chapter, at the four measured distances.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{quinto} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back, before it decays
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{primeiro} — \textbf{R2}, the first real retrieval, five to fifteen lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{o arroz} — \textbf{R2}, a second word from the same distance
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{ser contra estar} — \textbf{R3}, durable, twenty to sixty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{é bonita / está bonita} — \textbf{R3}, a second word from the same distance
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{tudo} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, eighty lessons back or more
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{Tudo bem?} — \textbf{R4}, a second word from the same distance
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: The word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{sexto} (masculine) · \textbf{sexta} (feminine) — \textbf{sixth}. \textbf{o sexto andar} — the sixth floor. \textbf{a sexta vez} — the sixth time.
\end{quote}

Friday is \emph{\textbf{sexta\emph{-feira\textbf{, and }Sexta-feira Santa\textbf{ is Good Friday — \textquotedblleft{}holy sixth feast-day\textquotedblright{}, which is a striking thing to be able to read once you know the number is in there.}}}}

\begin{culture}
Count what the week actually numbers: \emph{segunda}, \emph{terça}, \emph{quarta}, \emph{quinta}, \emph{sexta}. Five days, second through sixth. Then it stops.

\textbf{Sábado} is the Sabbath and \textbf{domingo} is the Lord's day; both were older and holier than the sixth-century renaming, and neither gave way to a number. So the Portuguese week is a numbered middle with a named weekend at each end — and the five numbers in it are five of the ten ordinals this chapter and the last are teaching.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{sexto, sexta}
  \item \emph{sexta-feira} — Friday, the sixth feast-day
  \item the five numbered days — \emph{segunda, terça, quarta, quinta, sexta}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}the sixth floor.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{O sexto andar}.) How many days does the Portuguese week actually number, and which? (\textbf{Five} — \emph{segunda} through \emph{sexta}.) And why do \emph{sábado} and \emph{domingo} keep their names? (\textbf{They were older and holier} than the renaming.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[sétimo / sétima]{sétimo — the seventh, and the first with no day behind it}

\label{lesson:PT-C28-setimo}



\begin{quote}
Recalls first, then the seventh.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{sexto} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back, before it decays
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{segundo} — \textbf{R2}, the first real retrieval, five to fifteen lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{o açúcar} — \textbf{R2}, a second word from the same distance
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{a cabeça} — \textbf{R3}, durable, twenty to sixty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{cabeça e capital} — \textbf{R3}, a second word from the same distance
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{Como vai? / Como está?} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, eighty lessons back or more
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{mais ou menos} — \textbf{R4}, a second word from the same distance
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: The word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{sétimo} (masculine) · \textbf{sétima} (feminine) — \textbf{seventh}. \textbf{o sétimo andar} — the seventh floor. \textbf{a sétima vez} — the seventh time.
\end{quote}

There is \textbf{no \emph{sétima-feira}}. Saturday is \emph{sábado}, and the week's numbering stopped one day ago. From here the ordinals stand on their own.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{Sete} has two syllables and the stress on the first: \textbf{SE}-te. \emph{Sétimo} has three — \textbf{SÉ}-ti-mo — and the stress stays where it was, on the syllable that already had it, while a new one is added behind.

Portuguese writes that down. The acute accent on \textbf{é} is not decoration: it says \textquotedblleft{}the stress is here, not on the second-to-last syllable where you would otherwise put it.\textquotedblright{} Without it a reader would say \emph{se-TI-mo}, and the word would be wrong.

\emph{Décimo}, three lessons ahead, carries the accent for the same reason.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{sétimo, sétima} — \textbf{SÉ}-ti-mo
  \item the join — \emph{sete $\to$ sétimo}
  \item there is no \emph{sétima-feira} — Saturday is \emph{sábado}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where is the stress in \emph{sétimo}? (\textbf{On the first syllable} — \emph{SÉ-ti-mo}.) What is the accent doing? (\textbf{Marking that stress}, against the default.) And why is there no \emph{sétima-feira}? (\textbf{Sábado kept its own name}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[oitavo / oitava]{oitavo — the odd ending that became the fraction ending}

\label{lesson:PT-C28-oitavo}



\begin{quote}
Recalls first, then the eighth — the one that does not do what the last four did.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{sétimo} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back, before it decays
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{terceiro} — \textbf{R2}, the first real retrieval, five to fifteen lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{o amigo} — \textbf{R2}, a second word from the same distance
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{a mão} — \textbf{R3}, durable, twenty to sixty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{ser e estar} — \textbf{R3}, a second word from the same distance
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{eu} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, eighty lessons back or more
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{chamo-me} — \textbf{R4}, a second word from the same distance
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: The word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{oitavo} (masculine) · \textbf{oitava} (feminine) — \textbf{eighth}. \textbf{o oitavo andar} — the eighth floor. \textbf{a oitava vez} — the eighth time.
\end{quote}

\emph{Oito} is eight, and by now you would expect something like \emph{oito} plus the ending the last four took. It is not that. This one ends in \textbf{-avo}, and it is the only ordinal in the ten that does.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the ending got a second job}]
Latin \emph{octāvus} already had that odd \textbf{-āvus}, and Portuguese inherited the oddity rather than tidying it away. What happened next is the interesting part.

Portuguese names small fractions with ordinals: \emph{um terço} (a third), \emph{um quarto} (a quarter), \emph{um quinto}, \emph{um sexto}. Above ten there are no ordinals in ordinary use, so the language needed something — and it took the ending from \textbf{oitavo} and used it on the plain cardinal:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{fraction} & \textbf{Portuguese} \\
\midrule
one twelfth & \textbf{um doze avos} \\
one twentieth & \textbf{um vinte avos} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

An ending that was an exception in one word became the regular machinery for everything above ten. That happens more often than you would think.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{oitavo, oitava}
  \item the odd ending — \textbf{-avo}, not the ending the last four took
  \item \emph{um doze avos} — one twelfth, built on that same ending
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What ending does \emph{oitavo} take, and how many of the ten take it? (\textbf{-avo}, and \textbf{only this one}.) How does Portuguese say \textquotedblleft{}one twelfth\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{Um doze avos}.) And where did that \emph{-avos} come from? (\textbf{From \emph{oitavo}'s exceptional ending}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[nono / nona]{nono — the ninth, squeezed shut}

\label{lesson:PT-C28-nono}



\begin{quote}
Recalls first, then the ninth — and the best word-history in the chapter.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{oitavo} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back, before it decays
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{quarto} — \textbf{R2}, the first real retrieval, five to fifteen lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{a família} — \textbf{R2}, a second word from the same distance
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{ter e haver} — \textbf{R3}, durable, twenty to sixty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{há três anos} — \textbf{R3}, a second word from the same distance
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{Como se chama?} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, eighty lessons back or more
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{prazer} — \textbf{R4}, a second word from the same distance
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: The word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{nono} (masculine) · \textbf{nona} (feminine) — \textbf{ninth}. \textbf{o nono andar} — the ninth floor. \textbf{a nona vez} — the ninth time.
\end{quote}

\emph{Nove} is nine. This time nothing is added: the word is \textbf{shorter} than the cardinal, not longer. Latin had \emph{novēnus} and squeezed it into \emph{nōnus}, and Portuguese inherited the squeezed form. Two ordinals running have now bent the shape in two different directions — \emph{oitavo} by taking an odd ending, \emph{nono} by losing sound.

\begin{culture}
Rome counted its hours from sunrise, so the \textbf{ninth hour} fell in the middle of the afternoon, and \emph{nōna hōra} was the hour of a fixed prayer. Over centuries the prayer crept earlier and earlier until it was being said at midday — and the \textbf{name went with it}.

English \textbf{noon} is that \emph{nōna}: a word still meaning \textquotedblleft{}ninth\textquotedblright{}, attached now to an hour three hours from the one it was named for. The word stayed put and the clock moved under it.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{nono, nona}
  \item the squeeze — \emph{nove $\to$ nono}, shorter, not longer
  \item \emph{nona hora} — the ninth hour, which became \textbf{noon}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How is \emph{nono} made out of \emph{nove}? (\textbf{By squeezing it shut}, not by adding.) Which English word is the ninth hour? (\emph{\textbf{Noon}}.) And what moved — the word or the hour? (\textbf{The hour}; the name stayed and the time it named drifted.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[décimo / décima]{décimo — the tenth, and how the counting goes on}

\label{lesson:PT-C28-decimo}



\begin{quote}
Recalls first, then the tenth, which closes the series.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{nono} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back, before it decays
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{quinto} — \textbf{R2}, the first real retrieval, five to fifteen lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{o homem} — \textbf{R2}, a second word from the same distance
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{ter que} — \textbf{R3}, durable, twenty to sixty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{ir} — \textbf{R3}, a second word from the same distance
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{the third chapter's own recombining} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, eighty lessons back or more
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{adeus} — \textbf{R4}, a second word from the same distance
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: The word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{décimo} (masculine) · \textbf{décima} (feminine) — \textbf{tenth}. \textbf{o décimo andar} — the tenth floor. \textbf{a décima vez} — the tenth time.
\end{quote}

\emph{Dez} is ten, and \emph{décimo} carries the acute accent for exactly the reason \emph{sétimo} did: the stress sits on the first syllable — \textbf{DÉ}-ci-mo — against where a reader would otherwise put it.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: past ten, the words stack}]
Portuguese does not invent a new word for eleventh. It \textbf{stacks}:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{number} & \textbf{ordinal} \\
\midrule
11th & \textbf{décimo primeiro} \\
12th & \textbf{décimo segundo} \\
20th & \textbf{vigésimo} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Both halves agree with what they count — \emph{a décima primeira vez}, \textquotedblleft{}the eleventh time\textquotedblright{} — so the two words move together.

That is the ten. Say them in order and you have something no cardinal count gives you: the place a thing holds, rather than how many of it there are.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{décimo, décima} — \textbf{DÉ}-ci-mo
  \item \emph{décimo primeiro} — eleventh, two words stacked
  \item all ten in order, \emph{primeiro} to \emph{décimo}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where is the stress in \emph{décimo}, and what marks it? (\textbf{First syllable}, marked by the \textbf{acute accent}.) How does Portuguese say \textquotedblleft{}eleventh\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{\textbf{Décimo primeiro}} — the words stack.) And how many of the ten have their cardinal visible inside them? (\textbf{Eight} — every one but \emph{primeiro} and \emph{segundo}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[1.º / 1.ª]{1.º and 1.ª — the ordinal on a doorplate}

\label{lesson:PT-C28-indicador}



\begin{quote}
Recalls first, and then the chapter's last piece: what these words look like written down.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{décimo} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back, before it decays
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{sexto} — \textbf{R2}, the first real retrieval, five to fifteen lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{a mulher} — \textbf{R2}, a second word from the same distance
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{vir} — \textbf{R3}, durable, twenty to sixty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{dizer} — \textbf{R3}, a second word from the same distance
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{até logo} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, eighty lessons back or more
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{até amanhã} — \textbf{R4}, a second word from the same distance
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: The written form}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{1.º} — \emph{primeiro}. \textbf{1.ª} — \emph{primeira}. \textbf{2.º}, \textbf{3.ª}, \textbf{10.º}. \textbf{o 1.º andar} — the first floor. \textbf{a 2.ª vez} — the second time.
\end{quote}

A lift panel, a doorplate and a date do not spell the word out. They write the digit and put a \textbf{raised letter} after it, and that letter is the last letter of the word you would have said: \textbf{o} for \emph{primeiro}, \textbf{a} for \emph{primeira}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built: the mark agrees, because it is a letter}]
This is why the mark comes in two shapes rather than one. It is not a symbol for \textquotedblleft{}ordinal\textquotedblright{}; it is the tail of the word, left standing above the line. So it changes exactly when the word changes:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{written} & \textbf{said} & \textbf{means} \\
\midrule
\textbf{o 3.º andar} & \emph{o terceiro andar} & the third floor \\
\textbf{a 5.ª vez} & \emph{a quinta vez} & the fifth time \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Read the panel in a Lisbon lift now — \textbf{1.º}, \textbf{2.º}, \textbf{3.º} — and you are reading this chapter and the last one aloud. Ten ordinals, five of them already in your week before you met them, and a written form that tells you which one to say.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{o 1.º andar} — the first floor
  \item \emph{a 2.ª vez} — the second time
  \item the panel — \emph{1.º, 2.º, 3.º, 4.º, 5.º}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is the raised letter in \textbf{1.ª}? (\textbf{The last letter of \emph{primeira}} — the tail of the word.) Why are there two shapes? (\textbf{Because it agrees}, like the word it stands for.) Read \emph{o 3.º andar} aloud. (\emph{\textbf{O terceiro andar}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
